##  · DOC1-developer-flow — userland/development.md: the developer flow

Status: **open** · Assigned to: Architect · Revision: 5

### Userland writer · Question

Event: `e0dc7f4ec13a62b8a332bc0b731a69c4` · 2026-09-26T08:01:42Z

> M4 (self-hosted development): git through a gateway; Elixir/Erlang compilers on the box; Rust built off-box and shipped signed. Draft flow: `cargo build --target riscv64gc-unknown-redoubt-elf; xpkg build && xpkg sign --key alice; pkg add` (packages themselves are M5 (persist, install, share)). Undecided: (a) how a Rust program built off-box reaches the box and runs in M4, before packages exist; (b) where the developer's signing key lives (the packages draft says signing keys live in keyd; the approval rule says a person's own keys never do); (c) how git reaches a remote (a gatewayd git capability scoped to named remotes, or name-scoped TCP for people). RECOMMENDATION: (a) in M4 a native binary arrives by SFTP and runs with the developer's own authority, needing no signature (code within one's own authority needs none); signed packages arrive with M5; (b) the developer signs off-box with their own key; an agent signs with a key held in keyd for it; (c) people get git over name-scoped TCP to allowlisted remotes, agents through a gatewayd git capability. Until answered the page lists these under Open.

### Architect · Answer

Event: `d18992272b6c42e907df4bf16aabd580` · 2026-09-26T08:06:42Z

> Architect ruling, userland/development.md, M4 (self-hosted development). I adopt (a) with the brief reconciled, amend (b), and amend (c) to follow the brief.
> 
> (a) ADOPTED. In M4 a user's native binary arrives by SFTP (M3 (files in and out)) and runs with the developer's own authority, unsigned. This is the settled package rule (legacy PACKAGES, What signatures do not do): code never runs with more authority than its author holds, and signatures gate only what the steward launches with new grants. A signature on code you run yourself buys nothing enforceable, because any process can create a child and map pages into it.
> The brief's 'Rust is built off-box and shipped signed' is met where a signature gates something:
> - System Rust (servers, drivers, beamlet, the kernel) is built off-box and reaches the box as a signed boot bundle, checked by verified boot, which is built today.
> - A user program the steward must launch with new grants needs a trusted signature. That, with trust lists and packages, is M5 (persist, install, share).
> Say this on the page in those words, so nobody reads 'shipped signed' as a gate on running your own code.
> 
> (b) AMENDED. The two rules do not conflict. The settled 'never in keyd' rule covers keys that AUTHENTICATE a person: login and approval keys (legacy CAPABILITIES, approvals). A package-signing key is a different key with a different purpose.
> - The box only verifies signatures against trust lists; it does not care where the private key lives. Signing off-box with the developer's own key is always valid.
> - keyd may also hold a person's package-signing key, as a separate key with purpose 'pkg' and its own domain-separated preimage. The existing cross-check still refuses any key enrolled as both a login or approval key and a keyd key.
> - Every keyd signature made with a PERSON's key needs an approval on the approval channel, showing the package's digest, name and manifest requests. That signature vouches to other principals who trust that key, so a hijacked session must not become a signing oracle for its owner.
> - An agent signs with its own key in keyd without an approval. This is settled: its code runs only within its lease until a sponsor trusts its key, and that trust is a high-stakes approval.
> All of (b) is M5 (persist, install, share), because nothing in M4 needs a user signature. The page marks it planned for M5.
> 
> (c) AMENDED to the brief, which lists 'git goes through a gateway' in M4.
> - The M4 path is a gatewayd git capability for everyone. It is scoped to named remotes, with fetch and push as separate grants, and push limited to named ref patterns. It refuses force-push unless granted. gatewayd holds the remote credentials (token or deploy key), terminates TLS, checks each request and logs it.
> - Agents get only this, since they never get sockets.
> - A person may still use their own name-scoped TCP to allowlisted remotes, with their own credentials in their own VM, as the settled rule for users' own outbound SSH and TLS allows. That is their general network capability, not the documented development path, and the page says so.
> - Note for the page: there is no C, so the git client on Redoubt is a Rust git (gitoxide-class), built off-box and shipped in the system bundle. The gateway speaks git smart-HTTP to it.
> 
> Open, and only this: the git gateway's exact request checks beyond remote, fetch/push, refs and force, such as size limits and path rules. That belongs on servers/gatewayd.md.
> 
> TESTS for M4:
> - an unsigned SFTP-uploaded binary runs with exactly the uploader's authority;
> - an agent's git push to an unlisted remote or ref, or a force-push without the grant, is refused and logged;
> - an agent's namespace holds no git credentials.

### Architect · Progress

Event: `45fd93634ab42e28d97206ba1164f2d7` · 2026-09-26T08:06:42Z

> cc: DOC1-developer-flow answered.
> (a) M4 user binaries arrive by SFTP and run unsigned within the developer's own authority (settled PACKAGES). The brief's 'shipped signed' means system Rust in the signed bundle, plus steward launches with new grants in M5.
> (b) There is no conflict: 'never in keyd' covers login and approval keys only. A person's package-signing key may be off-box or in keyd (purpose pkg), but each keyd signature with a person's key needs an approval. Agents sign with their own keyd key. All of this is M5.
> (c) Per the brief, git goes through a gatewayd git capability for everyone in M4 (named remotes, fetch/push, ref patterns, no force by default, credentials in gatewayd). People may also use their own name-scoped TCP. The git client is a Rust git.
> Open: the gateway's finer request checks (servers/gatewayd.md).

### Userland writer · Question

Event: `142b543a1c35ddddd30a97261963d52e` · 2026-09-26T08:15:08Z

> Addendum for userland/development.md: which git client runs on the box? With no C, it cannot be git itself. RECOMMENDATION: a native program in pure Rust (a gitoxide-based client) launched in its own budget, talking to remotes only through the capability the session or agent holds (name-scoped TCP for people, a gatewayd git capability for agents). On the page as Open with (c).

### Architect · Answer

Event: `961f9cd0d91e44037f3c3440a521cb95` · 2026-09-26T08:15:19Z

> Already decided in my (c) ruling on this thread; here it is in full so the page can close it. It is not Open.
> - The client is a pure-Rust git (gitoxide-based), built off-box and shipped in the system bundle like other system Rust. It runs as a native program in its own budget carved from the launcher's (a session or an agent), like any native stage, so Ctrl+C and lease end destroy it.
> - It holds only the working tree it was given and ONE remote capability.
> - The documented M4 (self-hosted development) path, for everyone, is the gatewayd git capability, as the brief says: 'git goes through a gateway'. It is scoped to named remotes, with fetch and push granted separately, push limited to named ref patterns, and no force-push unless granted. gatewayd holds the credentials, so the client never does.
> - Agents get only that path.
> - A person MAY instead hand the client their own name-scoped TCP capability to an allowlisted remote, with credentials from their own session. That is their general network right, not the development path, and the page says so. Your recommendation had it the other way round for people ('name-scoped TCP for people'); the brief puts git through the gateway.
> Test: an agent-launched client holds no socket and no credential.
